KEY MESSAGE 1...
Mid-upper level clouds will stream in today ahead of a digging
trough and developing low pressure, though we should remain 
rain-free through the day with afternoon highs of 55-60.

This forecaster thinks it's fair to say "the party"...in this 
case, a prolonged period of relatively warm and dry weather to
start the fall...is over starting this evening. A cold front 
will sink south across the area late this afternoon into this 
evening, with deepening low pressure tracking just to our south
across the Upper Ohio Valley overnight tonight. As guidance 
finally converges on the final track/intensity of this low, rain
chances and amounts have been nudged up a bit as it's looking 
like the expected swath of rain just north/northwest of the low
will track right across our forecast area. This will be a 
rather compact system moving through fairly quickly, which will 
limit rain amounts to a point. However, there will be a brief 
period of low-mid level frontogenesis as thermal packing takes 
place just north-northwest of the low tonight which should 
support more organized/banded rain. There may be just a touch 
of elevated instability as well, which can support a bit of a 
convective component. The forecast has a swath of 0.20-0.40" of
rain focused on a Findlay-Cleveland-Erie line through early 
Thursday with a bit less outside of that. Locally higher amounts
over 0.50" are possible, with guidance still disagreeing
slightly on exactly where the greatest swath of rain tracks. 
Lows tonight are expected to fall into the low-mid 40s.

Unsettled weather continues area-wide beneath the deepening
upper-level trough  on Thursday as low pressure transfers to 
off the northern Mid Atlantic coast. As temperatures aloft
continue cooling through Thursday and sufficient synoptic
moisture lingers, lake effect showers are expected to develop
early in the morning and continue through the day. With
initially northeast winds the lake effect will focus south-
southwest of the lake, farther west/southwest into North Central
Ohio than is normal. Outside of the lake effect, an inverted 
surface trough extending into the Great Lakes behind the 
departing low pressure is expected to drop across the area 
Thursday afternoon or evening as an embedded shortwave aloft 
also rotates through the region. This will likely bring a more 
organized batch of showers to the entire area and also cause 
ongoing lake effect to briefly enhance with the trough passage.
Additional rain amounts Thursday will generally be under a 
quarter-inch, though it's possible locations near and just 
southwest of Cleveland see more due to lake enhancement. 
Temperatures will rise no more than a few degrees and may even
cool later in the afternoon, with highs staying in the 40s. It 
will be blustery with northerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... 
Once the inverted trough sinks south of the area Thursday
evening, shower activity is expected to become primarily lake-
driven for the end of the week and into the weekend. Upper
troughing will be deepest overhead Thursday night and Friday
before slowly weakening and moving east this weekend. Initially 
north-northeast winds Thursday night are expected to gradually 
back more northerly on Friday and more northwesterly through the
weekend. Conditions will be most conducive to lake effect 
overnight Thursday night through early Saturday beneath the 
heart of the upper trough. During this timeframe, 500mb 
temperatures will bottom out at around -30C over 12-15C lake 
waters as synoptic moisture lingers. The mid-levels will start 
to gradually warm and dry on Saturday, though it is expected to 
be a slow ramp down of lake effect with activity not expected to
completely end until Sunday night or early Monday when the 
surface ridge axis builds into the area. Outside of the lake 
effect, there may still be a few sprinkles or light showers 
across Northwest OH on Friday beneath the deep troughing aloft. 
Conditions should trend completely dry across western portions 
of the area for the weekend.

The main focus for more organized/intense lake effect is 
expected to be a connection to Lake Huron. This connection is
expected to initially set-up west of Cleveland (and perhaps
briefly as far west as Sandusky and Mansfield) Thursday night
into Friday. From there, it will gradually shift east across the
Cleveland metro area later Friday into early Saturday and into 
the more traditional snowbelt of far Northeast OH and Northwest 
PA through the weekend. Outside of this connection there will be
some less-organized lake effect at times. The most precip will
tend to fall in the higher terrain immediately downwind of the
lake given the short fetch. Lake effect will ebb and flow in 
terms of organized and intensity through the event as various 
subtle vort maxes or shortwaves rotate through. There are hints
